extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literature; writers interested in literary style and moral/philosophical prose
extracted.subtask_description: Critical guidance and exemplars on the qualities that make moral/philosophical prose and poetry resonant: naturalness, emotional tone, practicality, simplicity, and the use of nature and anecdote to convey ethical truth. Helpful for writers aiming to produce sincere, affecting, and stylistically powerful literary work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries jotted down from day to day, meant for no eye but his own, 'without the slightest attempt at style, with no care, even, for correct writing, not to be surpassed for naturalness and sincerity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal or meditative writing's chief virtue can be its unstudied, sincere tone: authenticity and straightforwardness can be more powerful than stylistic artifice. For writers: allow plainness where it yields emotional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposefulness — avoid unnecessary acts and thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Let nothing be done without a purpose.' 'The greatest part of what we say or do being unnecessary, if a man takes this away, he will have more leisure and less uneasiness... take away not only unnecessary acts, but also unnecessary thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prune superfluous actions, lines, and ideas. Ask of every element of a piece: 'Is this one of the unnecessary things?' Remove what doesn't serve purpose or meaning to increase clarity and emotional economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional accent that reaches the soul
rubrics_metrics.description: The morality 'acquires a special character' by its 'accent of emotion' — Marcus Aurelius's sentences 'find their way to the soul' rather than merely stimulating the intellect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for writing that suffuses moral or philosophical claims with feeling so they affect readers' hearts as well as minds; do not rely on rhetoric alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of sweetness and dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A just admixture in the moral character of sweetness and dignity' is singled out as a distinguishing and beautiful quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance gentleness and gravitas in tone: tenderness without weakness, dignity without coldness. This admixture makes moral writing attractive and persuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise, fundamental principles (brief maxims)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Let thy principles be brief and fundamental, which as soon as thou shalt recur to them, will be sufficient to cleanse the soul completely.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, clear, repeatable maxims or guiding ideas that can be readily recalled and applied; brevity in ethical instruction enhances its practical power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-examination and vigilance
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of asking 'About what am I now employing my soul?... whose soul have I now?' and the injunction to 'take care that thou dost not change these names' (good, modest, true, rational...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate continual inward questioning and the discipline of returning to chosen virtues; in writing, model and encourage reflective practice rather than complacency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal perspective on transience
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages advising to 'Look down from above on the countless herds of men...' and reminders that 'the things which are much valued in life are empty, and rotten, and trifling.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt and convey a broad, historical or 'view-from-above' perspective to deflate petty concerns and highlight what endures; use transience as a theme to reframe values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of social nature (social principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The prime principle in man's constitution is the social' and the counsel to 'think of the virtues of those who live with thee' when seeking delight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge human sociality in moral writing: consider community, duties, and the virtues of others as part of ethical reflection and depiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic motive for action (avoid seeking reward)
rubrics_metrics.description: Marcus's ideal: the man who does good 'is like a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks for nothing more after it has once produced its proper fruit' — contrasted with acting for recompense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray and encourage action done for its own sake, not for external reward or praise; dramatize interior motives rather than external incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid, tender natural imagery ('natural magic')
rubrics_metrics.description: Delicate observations — 'Figs, when they are quite ripe, gape open; and in the ripe olives the very circumstance of their being near to rottenness adds a peculiar beauty...' — exemplify 'natural magic' that pleases the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ close, affectionate observation of nature to evoke wonder and moral feeling; concrete sensory detail can carry philosophical or emotional weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and freedom from superfluity
rubrics_metrics.description: Praises 'simplicity in my way of living' and counsels 'freedom from trifling, no love of superfluity' among desirable qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor simplicity of expression and life; avoid rhetorical excess, ornamentation, or distractions that dilute the central moral or aesthetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicalness and actionable advice
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes 'a stringent practicalness worthy of Franklin' in Marcus's precepts and gives many 'practical rules' for conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend reflection with concrete, applicable advice or rules; writing that instructs how to act (not only how to feel) is especially useful to readers seeking guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of anecdote and social testimony to demonstrate character
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdotes (e.g., his speech on Avidius Cassius) and the presence of busts in private houses are used as evidence of Marcus's character 'in praise of his sincerity, justice, and goodness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support general claims about character or virtue with illustrative anecdotes, reputational evidence, or concrete episodes to make abstractions vivid and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of intellect and emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast: 'Sentences of Seneca are stimulating to the intellect; the sentences of Epictetus are fortifying to the character; the sentences of Marcus Aurelius find their way to the soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for a synthesis where intellectual clarity, moral force, and emotional resonance coexist; avoid privileging cold argument over feeling, or feeling over reason.
